title: German and Czech, beyond pilsner
lead: Kölsch and Altbier, the wheat and bock families, smoke beer, and the purity law.

video.title: My Favorite Beer Rivalry: Altbier vs Kölsch

read.where: **Kölsch** (4.4–5.2%) is very pale, brilliantly clear and delicately fruity: top-fermented, then cold-conditioned like a lager. Since **1986** the name is **protected** for breweries in and around **Cologne**, where it’s poured in a small **stange**. **Altbier** (“old beer”) from **Düsseldorf** is **copper**, dry and firmly **bitter**. Germans don’t split beer into ale and lager the way Americans do: they say **top- or bottom-fermented**, and “lager” means cold-aging.
read.mixup: Kölsch looks like a light lager, but it’s an ale: a hint of fruit gives it away.
read.sayIt: It’s a Kölsch: as light and crisp as a lager, with a touch of fruit.

read.where: **Dunkelweizen** (dark wheat, 4.3–5.6%) has Hefeweizen’s **banana and clove** yeast plus **toasted bread** and caramel malt. Old Bavarian wheat beer was usually dark; pale Weissbier only took over in the 1960s. **Weizenbock** (6.5–9%) is wheat beer brewed to **bock** strength: Schneider **Aventinus** (Munich, 1907) is the classic dark one, Weihenstephaner Vitus a pale one. Both go in the **weizen glass**.
read.mixup: Weizenbock isn’t a bock with a lemon. It’s a strong wheat beer with the same banana and clove.

video.title: What even is Doppelbock? | The Craft Beer Channel

read.where: **Doppelbock** (7–10%) is very **rich and malty**. Munich monks brewed it as “**liquid bread**” for the Lenten fast. Paulaner owns the name **Salvator**, so others named theirs with **-ator**: Ayinger **Celebrator**, Spaten **Optimator**, Tröegs Troegenator. **Eisbock** (9–14%) is made by **freezing** a doppelbock-like beer and removing ice, concentrating it. BJCP stresses the name describes the **process**, not the strength.
read.mixup: An “-ator” name almost always means doppelbock. It’s a naming habit, not a rule.
read.sayIt: It’s a doppelbock: rich, malty, about 8%. A sipping beer.

video.title: Beer Log: why Vienna lager is the Minidisc of beer | The Craft Beer Channel

read.where: **Rauchbier** (“smoke beer”) from **Bamberg** is an amber lager made with **beechwood-smoked** malt; Schlenkerla is the benchmark. **Vienna lager** (1841, Anton Dreher) is **amber**, soft and toasty but dry; Austrian brewers carried it to **Mexico**. The Czechs have **amber** (polotmavé) and **dark** (tmavé) lagers too, and label strength by **degrees Plato**: a “12°” is a ležák, the standard lager.
read.mixup: The 12° on a Czech label is its starting gravity, not its alcohol. A 12° lager is roughly 5%.
read.sayIt: It’s a smoked beer: think campfire, or smoked ham.

video.title: What is the German Beer Purity Law? | Made in Germany

keyPoints.line: added once people knew it existed.
part of the 1993 German beer law.

read.where: On **April 23, 1516**, Bavaria’s Duke Wilhelm IV decreed that beer could only contain **barley, hops and water**; **yeast** was added later, once it was understood. It became law for all of Germany in **1906**, and the name “Reinheitsgebot” dates from **1918**. Today it lives on inside Germany’s **1993** beer law. In **1987** the European Court ruled it couldn’t keep imported beer out, so foreign beer brewed other ways can be sold in Germany.
read.mixup: Wheat beer isn’t illegal in Germany. Top-fermented beers may use malted wheat.
